question: Pregnant women have been considered a particularly vulnerable group since the Thalidomide scandal. Yet, despite this, COVID-19 vaccines have already been administered without this group being included in the initial marketing authorisation studies. Meanwhile, there are reports of possible risks to pregnancy and fertility.

An analysis from Czechia found significantly lower rates of successful pregnancies in women vaccinated before conception1. Anthony Fauci also discussed a risk of miscarriage after vaccination in the first trimester as early as January 20212. The frequently cited miscarriage rate of 82 % comes from an analysis by Thorp et al. and was also discussed in the US Senate34. 1.
Since when have the Commission, the EMA and the ECDC been aware of possible risks of COVID-19 vaccinations for pregnancy, miscarriage and fertility?
With the lack of data available early on, why were pregnant women encouraged/recommended to get vaccinated?

Why have all precautionary measures in place for pregnant women since the Thalidomide scandal been overridden for the COVID-19 vaccinations and pregnant women been vaccinated up until now, and who bears political responsibility for this decision at EU level?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.10.2026) The Commission granted marketing authorisation to COVID-19 vaccines starting from 21 December 2020, based on a scientific assessment of their quality, safety and efficacy by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use.

Since then, more than 13 billion doses have been administered worldwide1, generating an unprecedented amount of real-world safety data. Several studies concluded that mRNA COVID-19 vaccines do not cause complications in pregnancy, either for expectant mothers or their babies2. The evidence shows that vaccination during pregnancy protects both mother and baby.

There is no scientific proof of any association between COVID-19 vaccines and fertility impairment3. Pre-authorisation clinical trials did not include pregnant women but recommendations for the use of vaccines evolved as safety data became available.

On 18 January 2022, the EMA issued a statement following a detailed review of several studies involving around 65,000 pregnancies at different stages, which did not find signs of an increased risk of pregnancy complications, miscarriages, preterm births or adverse effects in the unborn babies following mRNA COVID19 vaccination4.

National authorities and the EMA continuously monitor the safety of COVID19 vaccines to ensure any possible risks are detected and managed as early as possible5. The organisation and delivery of health services and medical care is a national competence6.

The EMA and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control issue recommendations based on available scientific evidence, providing Member States with technical knowledge to strengthen and support their vaccination policies. The Commission refers the Honourable Member to written question E-2794/20267.
6 Article 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. 7 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-002794-ASW_EN.html.
